content: Insulin lispro is prescribed to help manage blood sugar levels in individuals with diabetes. It belongs to a class of medications known as hormones. People with diabetes often do not produce sufficient natural insulin, which is essential for metabolizing carbohydrates, fats, and proteins from food and for transporting sugar from the bloodstream to other parts of the body. Insulin lispro works by replacing the insulin that the body would normally produce. It acts more quickly than regular insulin but has a shorter duration of action. It is always used in combination with other diabetes medications, which may include another type of insulin or oral medications, depending on the type of diabetes you have. Insulin lispro is available as a liquid solution for subcutaneous injection (under the skin). It is typically injected 15 minutes before a meal or immediately after eating. Your doctor will determine how many times a day you should inject it. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Use insulin lispro exactly as directed, and do not use more or less of it or use it more frequently than prescribed. Never use insulin lispro if you have symptoms of hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) or if your blood sugar is confirmed to be low. In such cases, contact your doctor immediately. Insulin lispro helps control diabetes but does not cure it. Continue using it even if you feel well, and do not stop without consulting your doctor. Do not switch to another brand or type of insulin or change your dose without your doctor’s approval. Insulin lispro is available in vials, cartridges for use in dosing pens, and prefilled dosing pens. Ensure you know the type of container your insulin lispro comes in and the supplies you need, such as needles, syringes, or pens, to administer your medication. If your insulin lispro comes in vials, you will need syringes marked U-100. If it comes in cartridges, you will need to purchase an insulin pen separately. Always read the manufacturer’s instructions for your pen and ask your doctor or pharmacist to demonstrate its use. If your insulin lispro comes in pens, follow the manufacturer’s instructions carefully, and always prime the pen before use. Never remove the cartridge from the pen or mix other types of insulin into the cartridge. Do not reuse needles or syringes, and never share them with others. Dispose of needles and syringes in a puncture-resistant container, and ask your doctor or pharmacist how to properly dispose of the container. Your doctor may instruct you to mix insulin lispro with another type of insulin in the same syringe. Always draw insulin lispro into the syringe first, use the same brand of syringe, and inject the mixture immediately after preparation. You can inject insulin lispro into your thighs, stomach, or upper arms. Rotate injection sites, ensuring each injection is at least half an inch away from the previous one. Inspect your insulin lispro before use; it should be clear, colorless, and fluid like water. Do not use it if it appears colored, cloudy, thickened, or contains solid particles, or if the expiration date has passed. To prepare a dose of insulin lispro from a vial, wash your hands, remove the plastic cap from a new bottle (but do not remove the stopper), and clean the stopper with an alcohol swab. Pull back the syringe plunger to the dose your doctor prescribed, inject air into the vial, and draw the correct dose of insulin into the syringe. Check for air bubbles and remove them if present. To inject the dose, clean the injection site with an alcohol pad, pinch or spread the skin, insert the needle, and inject the insulin. If using a pen, follow the manufacturer’s instructions for dispensing the dose. After injecting, press down on the site for several seconds without rubbing it. This medication may be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before using insulin lispro, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to insulin or any other medications. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking, as some may interact with insulin lispro. Mention any history of nerve damage caused by diabetes, adrenal, pituitary, or thyroid gland disorders, or liver or kidney disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while using insulin lispro, contact your doctor immediately. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental surgery, inform your healthcare provider that you are using insulin lispro. Ask your doctor how to adjust your insulin dose if you become ill, experience unusual stress, travel across time zones, or change your exercise or activity schedule, as these factors can affect your insulin needs. Your doctor will also advise you on how often to check your blood sugar levels. Be aware that hypoglycemia may impair your ability to perform tasks such as driving, and ask your doctor if you need to check your blood sugar before driving or operating machinery. Follow all dietary recommendations provided by your doctor or dietitian. Maintain a consistent diet, eating similar amounts and types of food at the same times each day. Skipping or delaying meals or altering your diet can disrupt blood sugar control. Alcohol can lower blood sugar levels; consult your doctor about the safe use of alcohol while using insulin lispro. If you forget a dose, inject it as soon as you remember, provided it is shortly before or after a meal. If significant time has passed since your meal, contact your doctor for guidance. Do not inject a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Insulin lispro may cause changes in blood sugar levels. Be familiar with the symptoms of low and high blood sugar and how to manage them. Symptoms of hypoglycemia include shakiness, dizziness, sweating, irritability, mood changes, headache, numbness or tingling around the mouth, weakness, pale skin, hunger, and clumsy or jerky movements. Severe hypoglycemia can cause confusion, seizures, or loss of consciousness. Ensure those around you know how to respond to these symptoms and seek medical help immediately if they occur. Symptoms of hyperglycemia include extreme thirst, frequent urination, extreme hunger, weakness, and blurred vision. Untreated hyperglycemia can lead to diabetic ketoacidosis, a life-threatening condition characterized by dry mouth, upset stomach, vomiting, shortness of breath, fruity-smelling breath, and decreased consciousness. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience these symptoms. Common side effects of insulin lispro include redness, swelling, or itching at the injection site. Inform your doctor if these symptoms are severe or persistent. Rare but serious side effects include rash, difficulty breathing or swallowing, hives, wheezing, rapid heartbeat, skin changes (thickening or indentations), muscle weakness, tingling in the limbs, constipation, stomach cramps, or depression. Report any unusual problems to your doctor. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch program. Store insulin lispro in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Refrigerate vials, pens, and cartridges not in use, but do not freeze them. The vial or pen you are using can be stored at room temperature in a cool, dark place for up to 28 days. Discard expired or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for disposal instructions. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call 911 if the person collapses or is not breathing. Overdose can cause hypoglycemia, which may lead to coma or seizures. Follow your doctor’s instructions for managing hypoglycemia if symptoms occur. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. Your doctor will monitor your response to insulin lispro through blood or urine sugar tests. Always wear a diabetic identification bracelet to ensure proper treatment in emergencies. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist about refilling your prescription.
